planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in midsummer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; site Chinese magnolia where its outward-nodding flowers can be viewed from below or on a slope.

directions: Chinese magnolia is a wide-spreading deciduous shrub or small tree from western Sichuan, China, introduced to Western gardens from plant-hunting expeditions in the early 1900s. In late spring, after the leaves emerge, it produces abundant, fragrant, saucer-shaped white flowers with a prominent boss of crimson-red stamens; the flowers nod or hang outward on their stalks rather than facing straight up, so they are best appreciated from below or from a vantage point on a slope. Its late flowering (after most other magnolias) largely avoids late-frost damage to the blooms. Give it a sheltered woodland-edge position in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil with some shade, similar to the closely related M. sieboldii and M. wilsonii.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; globe magnolia flowers after the leaves emerge in late spring to early summer, so late-frost damage to blooms is rare.

directions: Globe magnolia is a deciduous shrub or small tree native to the eastern Himalaya and adjacent southwestern China, closely related to M. sieboldii and M. wilsonii in the same pendant-flowered group. Its creamy-white, cup-shaped, fragrant flowers hang downward on slender stalks and are distinctive for the dense, rusty-brown, felted indumentum covering the bud scales and calyx, a soft fawn fuzz that persists as the flower opens. Flowers appear with or just after the leaves in late spring to early summer. Best sited in a shaded woodland garden on a slope or above a path so the nodding blooms can be viewed at eye level or from below; protect from strong wind and drying heat.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, choosing a site sheltered from the earliest hard freezes since it flowers very early.

directions: Zen's magnolia is an extremely rare deciduous tree known in the wild from only a small number of surviving trees in Jiangsu Province, China, making it one of the most critically endangered magnolias and a high priority for ex-situ conservation collections. It is among the very earliest magnolias to bloom, often flowering in late winter ahead of the related M. denudata, with fragrant white flowers flushed purple-pink at the base of the tepals opening on bare branches. Despite its rarity in the wild, it grows readily in cultivation and is slowly becoming more available through botanical gardens and specialty nurseries. Plant in full sun to light shade with good drainage; its very early bloom time means open flowers occasionally risk a late hard freeze.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; flowers open very early on bare branches, so avoid frost pockets and low-lying sites.

directions: Cylindrical-fruited magnolia is a Chinese deciduous tree closely related to the Yulan magnolia (M. denudata), producing fragrant white flowers flushed with purple-pink at the base of the tepals on bare branches in very early spring, before the leaves emerge. It takes its common name from its distinctively narrow, elongated, cylinder-shaped fruiting cones, which stand out from the rounder fruit clusters of most other magnolias and add interest into late summer. It grows into a broad, rounded tree over time and is valued by collectors as a hardy alternative to M. denudata with a similar early-season display. Plant in a sheltered site away from cold air drainage to protect the early flowers from late frost.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, in a sheltered site protected from hard freezes and drying winter wind.

directions: Delavay's magnolia is an evergreen tree from Yunnan and Guizhou, China, grown for its huge, leathery, blue-green leaves, among the largest and most dramatic foliage of any evergreen magnolia relative, rather than for a long bloom season. Large, creamy-white, bowl-shaped flowers with a heavy, sweet fragrance open in summer but are short-lived, typically lasting only a day or two per flower. It is less cold-hardy than Southern magnolia (M. grandiflora) and best suited to warm zone 8-10 gardens or a large container that can be moved under cover in hard freezes. Site it in a sheltered spot with shelter from wind to protect the oversized leaves, and allow plenty of room for its eventual broad, substantial canopy.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; star-like flowers open on bare branches in early spring, so avoid frost pockets.

directions: Anise magnolia is a Japanese deciduous tree notable for its narrow, willow-like leaves and aromatic bark and foliage, which release a distinct anise-like, citrusy fragrance when bruised or crushed, a feature unlike any other commonly grown magnolia. In early spring, before the leaves emerge, bare branches are covered with fragrant, star-shaped white flowers with six slender tepals, closely resembling star magnolia (M. stellata) but carried on a more upright, tree-like, pyramidal habit. It tolerates clay soil and partial shade better than many magnolias and makes a graceful specimen or small flowering tree for a woodland garden edge. Give it a sheltered site away from the latest spring frosts to protect the early flowers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; flowers open on bare branches very early in the season, so choose a site sheltered from the hardest late-winter freezes.

directions: Biond magnolia is a Chinese deciduous tree known for flowering extremely early, among the first of all magnolias to open, often well ahead of Yulan magnolia (M. denudata) in late winter. Fragrant, upright, tulip-shaped white flowers, sometimes flushed with purple-pink at the base of the tepals, open on bare branches before any other spring ornamental is in bloom. It grows into an upright, vigorous small tree and has been used in hybridizing programs seeking very early bloom combined with cold hardiness. Because flowering begins so early, open blooms are occasionally damaged by a hard late freeze, so a site away from cold air drainage is preferred.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or grafted trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a sheltered, sunny site away from frost pockets; seedling trees can take well over a decade to begin flowering.

directions: Dawson's magnolia is a large deciduous tree from Sichuan, China, introduced to Western cultivation by early twentieth-century plant collecting expeditions and prized by collectors for its large, nodding, pale pink flowers, which can reach 6-8 inches across and open on bare branches in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge. It is closely related to M. campbellii and M. sprengeri but remains rare and mostly grown in specialist and botanic garden collections, in part because seedling trees are notoriously slow to reach flowering age. Give it a large, open, sheltered site with room to mature into a substantial specimen tree, and protect the early flowers from late frost.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; large upright flowers open on bare branches in early spring, so site away from frost pockets.

directions: Wufeng magnolia is a Chinese deciduous shrub or small tree first described from Wufeng County, Hubei Province, in the 2000s, and quickly recognized for having among the largest and deepest-colored flowers of any deciduous magnolia, large, upright, goblet-shaped blooms in rich wine-red to deep reddish-purple, opening on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. Since its introduction to cultivation it has drawn strong interest from magnolia breeders for its exceptional flower color and size, and selections are gradually becoming available outside China. Give it a sheltered, sunny site away from cold air drainage to protect the early flowers from late frost.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with shelter from strong wind; the enormous leaves are prone to tearing in exposed sites, similar to bigleaf magnolia (M. macrophylla).

directions: Beaked magnolia is native to Yunnan, southeastern Tibet, northern Myanmar, and adjacent northeastern India, and is related to bigleaf magnolia (M. macrophylla) and houpu magnolia (M. officinalis) in the same large-leaved group. It bears the largest leaves of any magnolia species, reportedly reaching nearly three feet long, giving it a bold, almost tropical appearance, along with large, fragrant, creamy-white flowers that open with or just after the leaves. It is less cold-hardy than its North American and Chinese relatives in the same group and remains rare in cultivation outside specialist and botanic garden collections. Site it in a sheltered location protected from strong wind to prevent the oversized leaves from tearing, and allow generous room for its eventual size.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; flowers open with the leaves in late spring, well after the main late-frost risk has passed.

directions: Wieseneri magnolia (also sold as M. x watsonii) is an old garden hybrid between houpu magnolia (M. officinalis var. biloba) and Oyama magnolia (M. sieboldii), first raised in Japan and long grown for combining the large, bowl-shaped, intensely fragrant flowers of its officinalis parent with the attractive crimson stamen boss of sieboldii. The creamy-white, outward- to slightly downward-facing flowers open on arching branches in late spring, after the leaves have emerged, largely avoiding frost damage, and fill the garden with a strong, sweet fragrance. It forms a wide-spreading small tree or large shrub and performs well in the same partial-shade woodland conditions favored by its sieboldii parent.
